445: “Look, Your Majesty — there is a moon on the sea as well.”
447: “A reflection is a moon too. Like the Lay Priest and the Cloistered Emperor — on this sea, no one need say which of them is the shadow.”
448: That night you sing imayō before the shrine halls. The shrine maidens dance, and the sea wind stirs the lamplight.
449: Go-Shirakawa and Kenshunmon-in made their pilgrimage to Itsukushima in the 3rd month of Jōan 4; see the Gyokuyō.
450: Tokuko entered the palace as Go-Shirakawa's adopted daughter in the 12th month of Jōan 1; the Heike Nōkyō sutras were dedicated in Chōkan 2.
451: Bind the two houses through Norihito and Tokuko, and favour Shigemori
452: Two houses in one boat — how far can they sail together?
453: Quietly strengthen the Northern and Western Guards against a later day
454: A smile on the face, a blade in the sleeve
455: Devote yourself to compiling the Ryōjin Hishō
456: Leave all you have learned in this life to those who come after
460: In the 3rd month of Angen 2 you turn fifty. Hōjūji-dono celebrates your fiftieth year; the young men of the Taira house dance before you, Kenshunmon-in sits at your side, and the whole court looks on in envy.
461: In the 6th month an evil sore rises on her back. On the 8th day of the 7th month Kenshunmon-in dies, aged thirty-five.
462: You sit all night in the Saishōkō-in she had built. Jien would later write: while Kenshunmon-in lived, the realm was still at peace; once she was gone, there was no one left to stand between the Cloistered Emperor and the Lay Priest Chancellor.
463: “Your Majesty,” says Tokitada when he comes to mourn, his eyes red and swollen, “from this day the world will not be as it was.”
464: You gaze at the lamplight and understand that you are standing at a fork in the road.
465: Kenshunmon-in died on the 8th day of the 7th month of Angen 2. Her death marks the turning point in the rupture between Go-Shirakawa and Kiyomori; see the Gukanshō and the Gyokuyō.
466: After grief, resolve to take back the power of the In
467: Carry on her wish, and rule the realm together with Kiyomori
468: Requires deep goodwill between the two houses
469: Once bound the two houses; Taira ≥15
472: Sacred Palanquins and a Great Fire
473: It began in Kaga. Morotsune — deputy governor and younger brother of Fujiwara no Morotaka, Governor of Kaga — quarrelled with the monks of Yūsen-ji on Hakusan and burned their lodgings. Hakusan is a branch temple of Enryaku-ji. Morotaka and his brother are the sons of your favourite, *Saikō*.
474: On the 13th day of the 4th month the monks of Enryaku-ji carry the *sacred palanquins* of Hiyoshi and Hakusan down the mountain and lay their demand before the palace: Morotaka must be exiled. Taira no Shigemori's soldiers guard the Kan'in palace; their arrows strike the palanquins by mistake, and many shrine servants and monks are killed or wounded. The monks abandon the palanquins in the street and depart, and the capital is gripped by dread.
475: On the night of the 28th day of the 4th month a fire breaks out at Higuchi-Tomikōji. A great wind drives it on until it reaches the Greater Palace — the Daigokuden, the Chōdōin, the Daigakuryō all burn to ash. The capital calls it the *Tarō Fire*.
476: Saikō tells you, “All of this is the work of Meiun, the Tendai Abbot, stirring them up.”
477: On the Hakusan incident and Enryaku-ji's armed petition of Angen 3, see the Gyokuyō and The Tale of the Heike, book 1.
478: On the Great Fire of Angen (the Tarō Fire), see the Hōjōki and the Gyokuyō. The Daigokuden was never rebuilt.
479: Strip Meiun of his abbacy, exile him to Izu, and order Kiyomori to attack the mountain
480: The historical path. The mountain will grind its teeth
481: Punish Morotaka and his brother, and placate the mountain
482: Saikō will resent it, but the wrath of the palanquins can be stilled
486: On the road to Izu, Meiun is seized at Awazu in Ōmi by the monks of Enryaku-ji and carried back up Mount Hiei. You order Kiyomori to send troops against the mountain; Kiyomori's face clouds, and he agrees only grudgingly.
487: The mountain is quiet for now — but you know that the anger of Saikō and the other favourites has not quieted at all.
488: Late at night, at Shishigatani in Higashiyama, in the villa of *Shunkan*, superintendent of Hosshō-ji. Present are the Major Counsellor *Fujiwara no Narichika*, Saikō, the police lieutenant *Taira no Yasuyori*, Narichika's son Naritsune, and *Tada Yukitsuna* of the Settsu Minamoto. They say they have come to view the moon, but what they speak of is how to destroy the house of Taira.
489: When the wine is well along, Narichika rises and his sleeve knocks over a *sake flask*. In Japanese, the word for flask, heishi, sounds just like “Heishi” — the Taira.
490: 「平氏倒れ候ひぬ。」 (“The Heishi has fallen.”)
491: You cannot help laughing aloud: 「猿乐を仕れ。」 (“Perform us some sarugaku.”)
492: 「ああ、あまりに平氏の多う候に、もて酔ひて候。」 (“Alas, there are far too many Heishi — they have made me drunk.”) He rises and sets the flask upright.
493: “Well then — what shall be done with these drunken Heishi?”
494: “Take their heads!” Saikō snaps the neck of the flask in one motion.
495: The whole company roars with laughter. Only Tada Yukitsuna does not laugh.
496: The Shishigatani plot appears in The Tale of the Heike, book 1, “Shishigatani,” the source of the flask episode. Historians doubt whether Go-Shirakawa was present in person; the Gukanshō records the affair but only briefly.
497: “平氏” (the Taira) and “瓶子” (a sake flask) are both read へいじ (heiji).
498: Smile and say nothing, tacitly allowing them
499: The historical path. You say neither yes nor no
500: Sternly dismiss them and forbid them to speak of it again
501: Kiyomori will never know you were here
502: Issue an In-zen on the spot and order them to raise troops
503: Strike Rokuhara while Kiyomori is far off in Fukuhara
505: Send a secret messenger to Kiyomori the next day
506: Betray your favourites to buy the Lay Priest's trust
507: Angen 3 (1177), last day of the 5th month
510: At Shishigatani you write out the In-zen with your own hand: “Taira no Kiyomori usurps the government of the court; let him be hunted down.” Narichika takes it, his hand trembling slightly.
511: On the last night of the 5th month, the Northern and Western Guards, joined by warriors of the Settsu and Ōmi Minamoto, sweep down from Higashiyama on Rokuhara. Kiyomori is far away in Fukuhara; the capital is held by his sons Shigemori and Munemori.
512: But Rokuhara is not Shirakawa-kita-dono. The Taira house has built dozens of mansions here, with more than a thousand retainers. Torches form an unbroken line along the east bank of the Kamo.
513: The fighting lasts from midnight until dawn. From an upper chamber of Hōjūji-dono you watch the glow of fire in the direction of Rokuhara.
514: At daybreak word arrives: Shigemori has been wounded by an arrow, and the Taira commanders have fallen back to the Nishi-Hachijō mansion. Munemori sends an envoy to Hōjūji-dono, offering the ranks and offices of the whole house in exchange for Kiyomori's safety.
515: At daybreak word arrives: Tada Yukitsuna has turned his coat on the field, and the Northern Guard has broken. Narichika has been taken. Taira soldiers are marching on Hōjūji-dono.
516: This is an imagined line. In history, Tada Yukitsuna betrayed the plot before it began, and none of the Shishigatani conspirators ever took up arms.
521: Your secret messenger reaches Fukuhara before anyone else. Kiyomori reads the letter and is silent for a long while, then says only: “The Cloistered Emperor is a truly frightening man.”
522: On the 1st day of the 6th month, Tada Yukitsuna knocks at the gate of the Nishi-Hachijō mansion deep in the night and lays the whole Shishigatani plot before Kiyomori.
523: Kiyomori comes at once from Fukuhara to the capital. Saikō is arrested, and even under interrogation he reviles Kiyomori as “a man of base birth squatting in high office.” Kiyomori, in a fury, has his mouth torn open and has him beheaded on Suzaku Avenue.
524: Fujiwara no Narichika is Shigemori's brother-in-law; only because Shigemori pleads desperately for him does Kiyomori spare his life and exile him to Bizen. In the 7th month Narichika is thrown from a cliff at his place of exile — some say he died in a pit lined with sharpened bamboo stakes.
525: Shunkan, Taira no Yasuyori and Fujiwara no Naritsune are exiled to *Kikai-ga-shima* in the southern sea.
526: When Kiyomori comes to see you there is suspicion in his eyes, but he does not let it loose. You know nothing of Shishigatani — or so it appears.
527: “I shall hold Your Majesty's warning in my heart.” Kiyomori observes every courtesy, yet never once looks you in the eye.
528: “Father, if you would confine the Cloistered Emperor, first cut off Shigemori's head. 忠ならんと欲すれば孝ならず、孝ならんと欲すれば忠ならず — if I would be loyal, I cannot be filial; if I would be filial, I cannot be loyal.” At last Kiyomori relents.
529: The attack on Mount Hiei is quietly let drop.
530: On the exposure of the Shishigatani plot, Saikō's execution, Narichika's death in Bizen and the exile of Shunkan and the others to Kikai-ga-shima, see The Tale of the Heike, book 2, and the Gyokuyō.
531: Shigemori's remonstrance on loyalty and filial piety comes from “The Admonition” in The Tale of the Heike and may be a literary embellishment.
533: Kiyomori may not listen, but the court and the realm will see
539: The Empress Tokuko is with child. To pray for a safe birth the court declares a general amnesty, and the pardon envoys sail far to Kikai-ga-shima and bring back Naritsune and Yasuyori.
540: Shunkan's name is not on the letter of pardon.
541: The Tale of the Heike says that Shunkan followed the envoys' ship into the sea — the water past his waist, past his chest — clinging to the gunwale and begging, until at last the ship pulled away. He collapsed on the sand, stamping his feet on the ground and wailing without end. The world calls it *ashizuri*: the stamping of feet.
542: On the 12th day of the 11th month, Tokuko gives birth to a prince, *Tokihito*. You take the child in your arms — your grandson, and Kiyomori's grandson too. Kiyomori is so overjoyed he does not know what to do with himself, and weeps aloud outside the birthing chamber.
543: Prince Tokihito (Emperor Antoku) was born on the 12th day of the 11th month of Jishō 2.
544: Shunkan's abandonment on Kikai-ga-shima appears in The Tale of the Heike, book 3, “Ashizuri.” Shunkan died on the island the following year; his page Ariō crossed the sea to find him.
545: Issue a separate In-zen pardoning Shunkan
546: Kiyomori will overrule it, but Shunkan will know
548: He was exiled for your sake
551: On the 17th day of the 6th month of Jishō 3, Kiyomori's daughter *Moriko*, the Lady of Shirakawa-dono, dies at twenty-four. The Regents' estates held in her name are left, for the moment, without a master.
552: On the 29th day of the 7th month, *Taira no Shigemori* dies, aged forty-two. He was the only one of the Taira who could restrain Kiyomori — and the only one who truly respected you. His proprietary province of Echizen passes to his son Koremori.
553: Your favourites whisper among themselves: a heaven-sent chance.
554: “The Shirakawa-dono estates should go to Lord Motofusa's son; the province of Echizen should be taken back by the In. Your Majesty, this is a gift from Heaven.”
555: In Fukuhara, Kiyomori says not a word.
556: The deaths of Moriko and Shigemori and Go-Shirakawa's seizure of their holdings were the immediate trigger of the coup of Jishō 3; see the Gyokuyō and the Sankaiki.
557: Seize the Shirakawa-dono estates and take Echizen
558: The historical path. How will Kiyomori answer?
559: Let Koremori keep Echizen, and give Moriko's estates to Emperor Takakura
560: Yield ground to gain it; turn aside from the blade's edge
562: Thousands of Horsemen Enter the Capital
563: On the 14th day of the 11th month, Kiyomori rides into the capital from Fukuhara with several thousand horsemen. The city is thrown into chaos; people clutch their belongings and flee in every direction, and rumour says Kiyomori means to destroy the Cloistered Emperor.
564: On the 15th the Regent Motofusa is dismissed and exiled to Bizen; on the 17th, thirty-nine officials from the Chancellor Moronaga down are stripped of office. Motofusa's place goes to Kiyomori's twenty-year-old son-in-law, *Konoe Motomichi*.
565: You send the Hōin Seiken — Shinzei's son — to Kiyomori with the message: “From this day forth, I shall take no part in the affairs of state.” Kiyomori makes no reply.
566: On the 20th, Taira soldiers surround Hōjūji-dono.
567: “My father's command cannot be refused. I beg Your Majesty… to remove to Toba.” Munemori kneels below the steps, not daring to raise his head.
568: “Munemori — does your father know that I am the adoptive father of your sister Tokuko?”
570: On the coup of Jishō 3, see the Gyokuyō, the Sankaiki and The Tale of the Heike, book 3. Go-Shirakawa was confined at Toba-dono, and cloistered rule came to a halt.
571: Bow your head, enter the carriage and remove to Toba-dono
572: Summon the warrior-monks of the mountain and the Northern Guard to resist
575: Swear to Kiyomori never again to meddle in government
576: An oath is only another way of singing an imayō
580: Toba-dono lies south of the capital, a detached palace built by your father, the Toba In. Now only a handful of attendants remain, and Taira soldiers stand outside the gate.
581: Only Seiken is allowed in. Each time he comes he brings some news from the capital, and some old stories of his father Shinzei.
582: “My late father once said,” Seiken hesitates, “that Your Majesty was a benighted ruler with few equals in Japan or China.”
584: “He also said Your Majesty has two virtues: first, whatever you wish to do, you do it without regard for what anyone says; second, whatever you have once heard, you never forget.”
585: In the 2nd month of Jishō 4, Emperor Takakura abdicates in favour of the three-year-old Tokihito, who becomes *Emperor Antoku*. Kiyomori is at last grandfather to the Son of Heaven. In Toba-dono you listen to the distant bells, and begin to sing.
586: Shinzei's judgement of Go-Shirakawa as “a benighted ruler with few equals in Japan or China,” and the remark on his two virtues, are quoted in Kujō Kanezane's Gyokuyō, entry for the 16th day of the 3rd month of Juei 3.
587: Chant sutras and sing imayō each day, and wait for Heaven's moment
588: Even a caged bird can sing
589: Use Seiken's visits to pass secret letters in every direction
590: Enryaku-ji, the Minamoto of the provinces, your sons
594: Your third son, *Prince Mochihito*, is thirty now and gifted beyond most — yet because of the Taira he has never been granted the rank of imperial prince.
595: On the 9th day of the 4th month he conspires with the seventy-seven-year-old warrior *Minamoto no Yorimasa*, and in the name of “Prince Saishō” issues a *ryōji* to the Minamoto of every province: destroy the Taira. Minamoto no Yukiie, Yoshitomo's younger brother, disguised as a yamabushi, carries the mandate across the eastern provinces — Yoritomo in Izu and Yoshinaka in Kiso both receive it.
596: A letter from Prince Mochihito makes its roundabout way to Toba-dono. He asks his father: can this be done?
597: In Toba-dono, you know nothing of it.
598: In the 5th month the plot is exposed. Prince Mochihito flees to Onjō-ji, then on toward Kōfuku-ji in Nara. At the Uji bridge Yorimasa tears up the planking and fights the pursuers across the river; when his arrows are spent he falls back into the Byōdō-in. There, on the Ōgi-no-shiba lawn, he writes his death poem and cuts open his belly. Prince Mochihito is struck by a stray arrow before the torii of Kōmyōzen and dies.
599: Prince Mochihito's mandate was issued on the 9th day of the 4th month of Jishō 4; see the Azuma Kagami and The Tale of the Heike, book 4.
600: On Minamoto no Yorimasa's death poem and the battle at the Byōdō-in in Uji, see The Tale of the Heike, “The Prince's Last Moments.”
602: Secretly fund his army from your private wealth
603: Your son is fighting for you
608: On the 2nd day of the 6th month, Kiyomori suddenly proclaims the removal of the capital to Fukuhara. Emperor Antoku, the Retired Emperor Takakura and you are all carried off to Settsu.
609: You are lodged in a cramped board house, fenced on all four sides with wooden palings. In the capital they call it *Kago no Gosho* — the palace in a cage.
610: In the 8th month word comes from Izu: the exile *Minamoto no Yoritomo* has raised troops and killed the deputy governor Yamaki Kanetaka. Soon after he is badly beaten at Ishibashiyama, hides in the Hakone mountains, and escapes across the sea to Awa. In the 9th month *Yoshinaka* rises in Kiso, in Shinano. In the 10th month Taira no Koremori leads a punitive army east and faces Yoritomo's forces at the Fujikawa in Suruga. In the night a flock of waterbirds takes flight, their wingbeats like the roar of a vast army, and the Taira host breaks without a fight.
611: In the 11th month, amid discontent on every side, Kiyomori at last returns the capital to Kyōto. In the 12th month Taira no Shigehira is sent against Nara, which had sided with Prince Mochihito — the wind is high and the fire fierce, and Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji are burned to scorched earth. The *Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji* melts in the flames, and its head falls to the ground.
612: On the move to Fukuhara, the battle of Fujikawa and the burning of Nara, see the Gyokuyō, the Azuma Kagami and The Tale of the Heike, book 5.
613: The “Kago no Gosho” appears in The Tale of the Heike, book 5, “The Moving of the Capital.”
614: Urge Kiyomori again and again to return to the old capital
615: Kyōto is the Emperor's capital — and yours
616: Watch coldly and let them ruin themselves
617: The Taira are losing the people's hearts, step by step
618: After the burning of Nara, send a private envoy to console Kōfuku-ji
623: On the 14th day of the 1st month, the Retired Emperor Takakura dies, aged twenty-one.
624: In the 2nd month Kiyomori falls ill with a fever that will not break. The Tale of the Heike says they poured cold water from the Senju well of Mount Hiei over him, and it boiled into steam the moment it touched his body; when they sprayed it through pipes, the water scattered like flames.
625: On the 4th day of the intercalary 2nd month, Kiyomori dies, aged sixty-four. His last words: “When I am dead, build no halls or pagodas, hold no memorial rites. Only send out men at once to take Yoritomo's head, and hang it before my grave.”
626: “From this day forth, all matters shall proceed by In-zen.”
628: In the 8th month a secret memorial reaches you by a roundabout road from the east. It is from Yoritomo.
629: “Yoritomo harbours no thought of rebellion; he seeks only to strike down his lord's enemies. If it is not your wish that the Taira be destroyed, then let it be as in olden days, with the Minamoto and the Taira serving side by side: let the Kantō be under the Minamoto, the lands west of the sea at the Taira's disposal, and the provincial governors appointed from above.”
630: East and west, divided. You hand the memorial to Munemori to read.
631: “My late father's last command was that even if only one of his descendants survives, that one must leave his corpse before Yoritomo.”
632: Kiyomori died on the 4th day of the intercalary 2nd month of Yōwa 1; for his last words, see The Tale of the Heike, book 6, “The Death of the Lay Priest.”
633: Yoritomo's secret proposal for the coexistence of the Minamoto and Taira appears in the Gyokuyō, entry for the 1st day of the 8th month of Yōwa 1. Munemori rejected it, citing Kiyomori's dying command.
634: Press Munemori hard to accept a division of the realm between Minamoto and Taira
635: If it succeeds, the realm is split three ways, with the In at its centre
636: Go through the motions, and watch the two houses fight
637: Throw all the In's strength behind the Taira and crush the east
638: Do you loathe that exile from Izu?
641: Three times you summon Munemori, and three times he refuses, citing his father's last command. The Taira commanders take Yoritomo's memorial for a stalling ruse, and murmur that the Cloistered Emperor is in secret league with the east.
642: You understand that your In-zen is not yet weighty enough to hold down the fury of a whole house.
643: The proposal to divide the realm comes to nothing.
648: These two years bring drought, great winds and floods, one after another. The tribute from the western provinces has been cut off by the war; the grain roads from the east are blocked by the Minamoto. The starving dead lie everywhere in the capital.
649: Kamo no Chōmei writes in the Hōjōki that the Hōin Ryūgyō of Ninna-ji, seeing how many had died, vowed to write the letter “A” on the brow of every corpse, to bind each to the Buddha. From the 4th month to the 5th, in the Left Capital alone, he counted more than forty-two thousand three hundred.
650: Many of those lying in the road are dressed in brocade — nobles who have sold everything else.
651: Looking out through the blinds of your carriage from Hōjūji-dono, you see a child lying on its mother's body, sucking at her breast, not knowing that she is dead.
652: On the Yōwa famine, see the Hōjōki, the source of the figure of more than 42,300 corpses counted by the Hōin Ryūgyō.
653: Open the In's granaries for relief
654: The Treasury will empty, but people's hearts will remember
655: Commission Fujiwara no Shunzei to compile the Senzai Wakashū
656: In an age of chaos, steady it with letters — and remember those who are about to die
657: Hold rites to pray for rain, and make offerings to the temples
658: The affairs of gods and Buddhas lie beyond human power
659: Juei 2 (1183), 7th month, night of the 24th day
662: In the 5th month Taira no Koremori leads an army of a hundred thousand north, and at Kurikara Pass, between Etchū and Kaga, is struck by Yoshinaka in a night attack. It is said Yoshinaka tied torches to the horns of several hundred oxen and drove them into the Taira camp. The Taira army plunged into the deep ravine, and the dead were piled up like mountains.
